cim: PSU Introduces Artificial Intelligence Degree Pathways
cim_eredeti: PSU Introduces Artificial Intelligence Degree Pathways
szoveg_eredeti:
As part of the Maseeh College of Engineering and Computer Science, the Computer Science (CS) department at Portland State University now offers three academic tracks for students interested in Artificial Intelligence (AI) – a major, a minor and a graduate certificate.

According to Wu-chi Feng, professor and chair of the CS department, the process to introduce the new AI degree pathways started in 2024.

“Part of our job as faculty is to look farther ahead and start putting things in place that are needed,” Wu-chi Feng said. “Creating an AI degree is a pretty onerous process.”

During this process, PSU had to gain approval from the Higher Education Coordinating Commission (HECC), the Statewide Provost Council and the Portland State Board of Trustees. The new academic program’s proposal was ultimately approved on May 7, 2026, by HECC, and states an expected “significant” demand increase for students trained in AI over the next decade.

Among the new degree pathways, the Bachelor of Science in AI is being offered as a four-year degree within the CS department. The program introduces undergraduate students to AI and modern computing, building foundational skills needed to work with these technologies. Pursuing a graduate certificate in AI requires admission into the CS program, but can be completed as an individual certificate or alongside a masters or doctoral degree in CS. Additionally, the minor in AI was designed to be accessible across disciplines and can be pursued by students outside the Maseeh College of Engineering and Computer Science.

Wu-chang Feng, the undergraduate curriculum coordinator for the CS department, added that the minor in AI was introduced in part because developments in the technology have created more space for non-technical people to learn computing systems and how to utilize AI tools.

“AI is allowing us to expand computing to the masses, and that’s the motivation of the minor,” Feng said. “If you think about it, AI is enabling non-technical people to build computing systems.”

A goal of the new AI program is to make knowledge of AI tools, and their problem solving capabilities, more available to the PSU student body. According to Dr. Jingke Li, associate professor and associate chair of the CS department, faculty expertise in AI was already available within the CS department. However, the AI major, minor and graduate certificate were introduced to make that expertise available outside of the traditional CS degree pathway.

“These new degree programs [are] very well orchestrated because they tailor to all these different needs,” Li said. “[If] people want more technical detail, they can follow the AI major. If they want to help to add some AI techniques to their own field, they can do the minor. It’s still early, but we feel that this will attract many new students to our program.”

The minor in AI is expected to draw students from different majors at PSU, particularly because it doesn’t require extensive prior knowledge of computer programming. While still teaching basic programming knowledge, the minor was designed for students to understand AI/ AI tools rather than complex computer programming. Wu-chang Feng has already noticed a more diverse student body in AI 112 Generative AI Studio, the introductory course for the AI minor. Feng stated that only a third of students in AI 112 are CS majors, while another third come from other majors and then senior auditors seeking to stay up to date on AI.

“The first time we offered [AI 112], it was mostly CS students because it was offered as a CS course, but once we moved to an AI course designation, more people found it, and then realized that this was what they wanted: just to learn how to use AI to solve their own problems,” Wu-chang Feng said. “You bring the problems that you want to solve, whatever discipline you’re from, and then we’ll show you the tools that AI can bring to bear to solve that problem.”

While the new AI degree pathways are expected to serve a broader range of the student body, the CS department recognizes that AI technology is something that’s constantly evolving. The new major, minor and graduate certificate have been introduced in an attempt to keep up with the expected market demand for students trained in AI – but it’s not a program the CS department expects to be stagnant.

“One thing I would like students to know is that everything’s a moving target, and this department understands [that] we have to keep on shifting what we’re offering,” Wu-chang Feng said. “There is that critical mass in this department of people who are trying to get a grip on what AI is doing to our discipline.”
